text: Differentiating swine conditions with nervous signs: Edema disease — linked to weaning and diet change; caused by a toxin-producing E. coli strain that damages small blood vessels, especially in the brain. About 2 weeks post-weaning: can present as sudden death, or incoordination (drunken walk), convulsions, swollen eyelids, and loss of appetite with a normal temperature. Treatment: isolate the piglet in a quiet space and inject Sulfa+TMP or Enrofloxacin. Prevention: dilute high-protein (often >20%) weaning feed with 20% pregnant-sow feed to lower the protein ratio, limit feed to about 50 g per kg of bodyweight rather than free access, and chlorinate drinking water to reduce E. coli levels. Streptococcus — common in weaned piglets, sometimes found dead with no prior signs noticed; red conjunctiva, loss of coordination, lying on the side with convulsions, death within hours, temperature over 41°C. Treatment only works if started very early (hesitant walk or standing immobile in a corner): isolate in a quiet space, inject Dexamethasone first, then Amoxicillin. Prevention: disinfect the post-weaning pen before moving piglets in, and if one piglet is affected, mix Amoxicillin into the whole group's feed for 5 days. Aujeszky Disease — in piglets under a week old: hind-leg paralysis with dog-like sitting, or lying down and paddling, walking in circles, and convulsions; some die within hours with no signs at all; mortality is very high in this age group, and once nervous signs start, death usually follows within 24–36 hours. In post-weaning pigs, convulsions are NOT typical of Aujeszky — consider Streptococcus if fever is over 41°C, or Edema disease if temperature is normal. A supporting clue for Aujeszky on a farm is dogs/cats getting sick after eating raw meat from infected pigs (dogs: intense itching to the point of self-injury, jaw/throat paralysis, howling, death; cats: usually die too fast to show symptoms). Tetanus — usually from poor hygiene/technique during castration; permanent signs once they appear: hypersensitivity, stiff legs and muscles, an erect tail, and facial/ear muscle spasms; early treatment is high-dose penicillin daily. Newborn piglet trembling — a hallmark sign of CSF: muscle tremor visible only while piglets are walking (not while asleep), nervous shaking, incoordination, often dog-sitting posture. Rabies — from a bite by an infected dog or cat: difficulty walking, nose twitching, rapid chewing with excess salivation, muscle spasm and tremor, death usually within 3 days.
caveat: Rabies is a serious human health risk as well — any pig showing these signs after a dog/cat bite should be handled with extreme caution.
